To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) repetition enhancement constitutes a major component of repetition suppression, (ii) repetition suppression is systematically associated with stimulus-selective delay activation, (iii) the combination of repetition suppression, stimulus selective delay activity and repetition-enhancement constitutes a neuronal mechanism that can be functionally linked to priming.

(a) stimulus-selective delay-period activity is a ubiquitous feature of single-unit recordings during working memory delay tasks; (b) stimulus-selective activity during the working memory delay is associated to a widespread reduction of neuronal activity upon stimulus repetition (i.e., repetition suppression); (c) repetition enhancement is a ubiquitous feature in the single-unit recordings of working memory delay tasks, and is associated to the presence of stimulus-selective delay-activity; and (d) repetition enhancement, rather than repetition suppression

repetition suppression is typically associated with a) stimulus-selective delay activation (i.e., stimulus-elicited spiking activity in the absence of the stimulus) and b) repetition enhancement (i.e., an increase of spicing activity upon stimulus repetition).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neuronal correlates of primed behavior, a fundamental issue of cognitive neuroscience.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
